From scratch · file 1 of 14 · 113 lines of NumPy

Linear regression

Cost, gradient and gradient descent in about sixty lines, then checked twice — once against a numerical gradient, once against the closed-form least-squares solution.

Run it yourself
cd study/scratch/code
python3 01_linear_regression.py

Pure NumPy — no scikit-learn, no TensorFlow. Every code block below is read straight out of that file, and the output under it is what that exact block printed when this page was built. They cannot drift apart.

By the end you will have built a working multi-feature linear regressor, z-score scaling, and a gradient checker you will reuse in every later file.

🖼️The whole program in one picture

Eight houses, three features. Small enough that you can check any number by hand, which is the whole point of starting here.

"""Linear regression from scratch — no scikit-learn, no TensorFlow.

Run me:  python3 01_linear_regression.py

Everything here is C1 W1-W2 in about 60 lines of NumPy. The last section
checks the answer against scikit-learn, so you can see it really is the same.
"""
import numpy as np
Line by line, in plain words

Imports, and nothing else. Pure NumPy — no scikit-learn, no TensorFlow. Everything below is arithmetic you could do on paper if you had the patience and the time.

The pointThe goal of this file: predict a number. How much is this house worth? That is regression. File 02 will predict a class instead, and almost nothing else will change.

X is (m, n) — one row per house, one column per feature — and y is (m,). Every shape error you will ever hit in the assignments comes from losing track of those two lines.

# A tiny house dataset: size (1000 sq ft), bedrooms, age (years) -> price ($1000s)
X = np.array([
    [2.10, 3, 20], [1.60, 3, 15], [2.40, 3, 18], [1.42, 2, 30],
    [3.00, 4, 8],  [1.99, 3, 25], [1.27, 2, 40], [2.65, 4, 12],
], dtype=float)
y = np.array([400., 330., 369., 232., 540., 400., 200., 480.])
m, n = X.shape
print(f"m = {m} examples, n = {n} features")
Line by line, in plain words

Eight houses. Each one has three numbers describing it, and one number to predict.

the shapes, which are the thing to hold on to
m = 8exampleshow many houses — the number of rows
n = 3featuressize, bedrooms, age — the number of columns
X(8, 3)the table of houses
y(8,)the eight prices
The pointRows are examples, columns are features. That convention holds for the whole specialization, and almost every shape error you will hit comes from momentarily forgetting it.

Eight houses is far too few to build anything real. It is exactly the right number to check by hand, which is what this file is for.

output
m = 8 examples, n = 3 features

Three lines. X @ w produces all eight predictions at once and + b broadcasts the same number onto every one of them. There is no loop because there does not need to be one.

def compute_cost(X, y, w, b):
    """J(w,b) = (1/2m) sum (f - y)^2.

    X is (m, n), w is (n,), b is a scalar. X @ w is (m,) — one prediction per
    row — and + b broadcasts the same number onto all of them.
    """
    f = X @ w + b                    # (m,)
    err = f - y                      # (m,)
    return float(np.sum(err ** 2) / (2 * len(y)))
Line by line, in plain words

The cost squashes all eight misses into one number, so two candidate models can be compared.

f = X @ w + b cost = np.mean((f - y) ** 2) / 2predict everything, then average the squared misses
  1. 1X @ w — one dot product per house. (8,3) @ (3,) → (8,): eight predictions, in one operation.
  2. 2+ b — broadcasting adds the same bias to all eight.
  3. 3f - y — eight misses.
  4. 4** 2 — square them, so too-high and too-low both count as bad and cannot cancel.
  5. 5np.mean(...) / 2 — average, then halve.
The pointThe ÷ 2 is pure convenience. Differentiating a square brings a 2 down in front; putting a 2 underneath in advance means it cancels and the gradient comes out clean. It moves the cost's value but not where its minimum is, which is all that matters.

The only part worth staring at is X.T @ err. The maths says for each feature j, sum the error times that feature. Transposing X makes each feature a row, so one matrix–vector product does every feature at once. Shapes: (n, m) @ (m,) → (n,).

def compute_gradient(X, y, w, b):
    """The two partial derivatives, vectorized.

    dj_dw[j] = (1/m) sum (f - y) * x_j   ->  that is column j of X dotted with
    the error vector, for every j at once, which is exactly X.T @ err.
    """
    m = len(y)
    err = (X @ w + b) - y            # (m,)
    dj_dw = (X.T @ err) / m          # (n, m) @ (m,) -> (n,)
    dj_db = float(np.sum(err) / m)   # scalar
    return dj_dw, dj_db
Line by line, in plain words

Two lines of arithmetic that carry the entire idea of learning.

err = f - y dj_dw = (X.T @ err) / m dj_db = err.mean()
  1. 1err — how wrong each house was. Eight numbers.
  2. 2X.T — the transpose, which turns the table on its side so the shapes line up: (3,8) @ (8,) → (3,).
  3. 3That gives one slope per feature — each miss weighted by that house's value for that feature, then summed.
  4. 4err.mean() — the bias slope, with no feature weighting.
The pointWhy the feature weighting? Because a miss on a big house is stronger evidence that the size weight is wrong than a miss on a small one. The bias has no such factor because b affects every house equally, so no house's opinion counts for more.

Before trusting a hand-derived gradient, check it. Nudge one parameter by a tiny ε, see how much the cost moved, divide. If the analytic and numerical answers disagree beyond about 1e-6, the analytic one is wrong — this catches almost every derivative bug you will ever write.

def numeric_gradient(f, theta, eps=1e-6):
    """Central difference. Used only to prove the analytic gradient is right."""
    g = np.zeros_like(theta, dtype=float)
    for i in range(theta.size):
        up, dn = theta.astype(float).copy(), theta.astype(float).copy()
        up[i] += eps
        dn[i] -= eps
        g[i] = (f(up) - f(dn)) / (2 * eps)
    return g

w0, b0 = np.array([0.2, -1.0, 0.5]), 3.0
ana_w, ana_b = compute_gradient(X, y, w0, b0)
num_w = numeric_gradient(lambda w: compute_cost(X, y, w, b0), w0)
num_b = numeric_gradient(lambda bb: compute_cost(X, y, w0, bb[0]), np.array([b0]))[0]
print("analytic dj_dw:", np.round(ana_w, 6))
print("numeric  dj_dw:", np.round(num_w, 6))
print("max difference:", f"{np.max(np.abs(ana_w - num_w)):.3e}",
      "| db diff:", f"{abs(ana_b - num_b):.3e}")
Line by line, in plain words

This block is a test, and it is the reason to trust everything after it.

two independent ways to get the same slope
The calculus version
compute_gradient — the formula you derived. Fast, and capable of being silently wrong.
The measured version
Nudge one weight up a hair, nudge it down a hair, see how much the cost moved, divide. No calculus involved, so it cannot repeat a calculus mistake.
what this block printed
analytic[−795.83, −1150.94, −6547.42]from the formula
numeric[−795.83, −1150.94, −6547.42]from measuring
max difference3.9e−06floating-point noise, not an error
bias difference7.2e−07same
The pointThe measured version is far too slow to train with — it re-runs the whole cost twice for every weight — but it is exactly right for checking. This is a real professional habit: a wrong gradient does not crash. It trains happily and converges to the wrong answer.
output
analytic dj_dw: [ -795.832078 -1150.94375  -6547.42125 ]
numeric  dj_dw: [ -795.832078 -1150.943746 -6547.421246]
max difference: 3.931e-06 | db diff: 7.248e-07

Look at the ranges before and after. Age spans 32 while size spans 1.73 — a factor of nearly twenty, which means their gradients differ by nearly twenty and no single α suits both. Note the function returns μ and σ as well: those are part of the trained model and you must keep them to predict on anything new.

def zscore(X):
    """Return scaled X plus the mu and sigma you must keep for prediction."""
    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    sigma = X.std(axis=0)
    return (X - mu) / sigma, mu, sigma

Xs, mu, sigma = zscore(X)
print("\nbefore scaling, column ranges:", np.round(X.max(0) - X.min(0), 2))
print("after  scaling, column ranges:", np.round(Xs.max(0) - Xs.min(0), 2))
Line by line, in plain words

Look at what the columns actually contain before scaling.

column ranges
before[1.73, 2.0, 32.0]the range of each column
after[3.04, 2.83, 3.30]all comparable
The pointAge spans 32 while size spans 1.73 — roughly 18× wider. That single fact makes the cost surface a long thin canyon rather than a bowl.

In a canyon, a gradient step points across the valley rather than along it, so the path zig-zags; and α has to stay small enough not to bounce out, which makes the crawl slower still. Scaling turns the canyon back into something round.

Xs = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)subtract each column's mean, divide by its spread
The pointaxis=0 is doing real work in X.mean(0): it means “one mean per column”, which is one per feature. Use axis=1 and you would get one per house, which is meaningless.
output
before scaling, column ranges: [ 1.73  2.   32.  ]
after  scaling, column ranges: [3.04 2.83 3.3 ]

The two updates both use the old w and b, because both gradients were computed before either changed. Doing it any other way is the classic simultaneous-update bug — and it usually still converges, which is why it survives in so much code.

def gradient_descent(X, y, alpha, iters):
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    b = 0.0
    history = []
    for i in range(iters):
        dj_dw, dj_db = compute_gradient(X, y, w, b)
        w = w - alpha * dj_dw        # both updates use the OLD w and b,
        b = b - alpha * dj_db        # because both gradients were computed above
        if i % (iters // 10) == 0 or i == iters - 1:
            history.append((i, compute_cost(X, y, w, b)))
    return w, b, history

w, b, hist = gradient_descent(Xs, y, alpha=0.1, iters=2000)
print("\niteration      cost")
for i, c in hist:
    print(f"{i:9d}  {c:9.4f}")
print(f"\nlearned w = {np.round(w, 3)}   b = {b:.3f}")
Line by line, in plain words

Three lines, repeated 1,500 times. Watch the cost column.

what training printed
iteration 058,285the cost when every weight is still zero
iteration 200240.9almost all the progress, in the first 200 steps
iteration 600237.29refining
iteration 1200237.2592converged — nothing is moving
The pointThe shape is the important part: an enormous drop, then a long flattening. By iteration 200 it is 99.6% of the way there, and the remaining 1,300 iterations buy four decimal places.

That shape is what a healthy run looks like. If the cost ever rises between two iterations, α is too large — and that one rule is the most useful piece of debugging in the whole specialization.

output
iteration      cost
        0  58285.3121
      200   240.9076
      400   237.6069
      600   237.2931
      800   237.2625
     1000   237.2595

Scaling at prediction time uses the training μ and σ. Recomputing them from new data changes the meaning of every weight and quietly ruins the model.

def predict(x_raw, w, b, mu, sigma):
    """Scale with the TRAINING mu and sigma, never with new data's own."""
    return float(((x_raw - mu) / sigma) @ w + b)

house = np.array([2.0, 3, 22])
print(f"\n2000 sq ft, 3 bed, 22 yrs -> ${predict(house, w, b, mu, sigma):.1f}k")
print("training predictions:", np.round(Xs @ w + b, 1))
print("actual prices:       ", y)
Line by line, in plain words

The model is trained. Now use it.

2000 sq ft, 3 bed, 22 yrs→$365.0ka house it has never seen

And here it is against the eight houses it was trained on:

training predictions vs. the truth (in $1000s)
predicted372, 336, 394, 229, 531, 364, 219, 506
actual400, 330, 369, 232, 540, 400, 200, 480
The pointIt is close but nowhere near exact — house 1 is out by 28, house 6 by 36. That is correct behaviour, not failure. A model that hit all eight exactly would have memorised eight houses and learned nothing about houses in general.

New input must be scaled with the same mean and standard deviation the training used. Feeding a raw 2000 into a model trained on standardised inputs returns nonsense, silently.

output
2000 sq ft, 3 bed, 22 yrs -> $365.0k
training predictions: [372.2 336.2 393.7 229.4 530.7 364.4 218.9 505.6]
actual prices:        [400. 330. 369. 232. 540. 400. 200. 480.]

The real test. np.linalg.lstsq solves for w and b directly, with no learning rate and no iterations. Undo our scaling and the two answers agree to three decimal places — so the sixty lines above really do compute linear regression, and not merely something that looks like it.

# The closed-form solution (the "normal equation") for comparison.
Xb = np.c_[np.ones(m), X]                       # add a column of 1s for b
theta = np.linalg.lstsq(Xb, y, rcond=None)[0]   # least squares, solved directly
print("\nnormal equation  b, w:", np.round(theta, 3))
# Undo the scaling on our gradient-descent answer so the two are comparable
w_unscaled = w / sigma
b_unscaled = b - float(w @ (mu / sigma))
print("gradient descent b, w:", np.round(np.r_[b_unscaled, w_unscaled], 3))
print("agree to 3 dp:", np.allclose(theta, np.r_[b_unscaled, w_unscaled], atol=1e-3))
Line by line, in plain words

The final check, and the most convincing one in the file. Linear regression has a closed-form solution — the normal equation — that gets the exact answer in one step with no iteration at all.

two completely different methods, one answer
normal equation[−61.281, 71.749, 94.137, 0.019]solved directly
gradient descent[−61.280, 71.750, 94.137, 0.019]1,500 small steps
agree to 3 dpTrue
The pointSo the sixty lines above really do compute linear regression, and not merely something that looks like it. Two independent methods arriving at the same four numbers is about as strong a check as you get.

Then why bother with gradient descent, if a formula solves it exactly? Because the normal equation needs to invert a matrix, which costs roughly n³ and becomes impossible past a few thousand features — and because it exists only for linear regression. Gradient descent works on everything in the rest of this specialization.

output
normal equation  b, w: [-6.1281e+01  7.1749e+01  9.4137e+01  1.9000e-02]
gradient descent b, w: [-6.1280e+01  7.1750e+01  9.4137e+01  1.9000e-02]
agree to 3 dp: True

From scratch · file 2 of 14 · 135 lines of NumPy

Logistic regression and regularization

The same skeleton as file 01 with three substitutions — a sigmoid, a log loss, and a λ term — plus a numerical trap that bites in real code.

Run it yourself
cd study/scratch/code
python3 02_logistic_regression.py

Pure NumPy — no scikit-learn, no TensorFlow. Every code block below is read straight out of that file, and the output under it is what that exact block printed when this page was built. They cannot drift apart.

By the end you will have built a regularized logistic classifier, an overflow-proof sigmoid, and a demonstration of the hidden constraint between α and λ.

🖼️The whole program in one picture

Eighty students, two exam scores, pass or fail. Two overlapping blobs so the problem is not trivially separable.

"""Logistic regression from scratch — C1 W3 in NumPy.

Run me:  python3 02_logistic_regression.py

Same skeleton as linear regression. Three things change: a sigmoid on the
output, log loss instead of squared error, and a lambda term on w.
"""
import numpy as np
Line by line, in plain words

The file opens by importing NumPy and nothing else. No scikit-learn, no TensorFlow — everything below is arithmetic you could do by hand if you had the patience.

Worth naming the goal before the code starts. File 01 answered “how much?” — a house is worth $420,000. This file answers “which of two?” — this student passes, that one does not. Everything that changes, changes because of that.

Forty of each class, deliberately overlapping — a perfectly separable dataset would let the weights grow without limit and hide what λ does.

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# Two blobs: exam scores of students who passed (1) and failed (0)
neg = rng.normal([45, 50], 12, size=(40, 2))
pos = rng.normal([70, 72], 12, size=(40, 2))
X = np.vstack([neg, pos])
y = np.r_[np.zeros(40), np.ones(40)]
m, n = X.shape
print(f"m = {m}, n = {n}, positives = {int(y.sum())}")
Line by line, in plain words

rng = np.random.default_rng(7) makes a random-number generator. The 7 is a seed: it means “use the same recipe for randomness every time”, so you and this page get the identical eighty students on every run. Change the 7 and you get a different class of students, and every number below shifts.

rng.normal([45, 50], 12, size=(40, 2)) invents forty students whose two exam scores hover around 45 and 50, give or take about 12. These are the ones who failed. The next line does the same around 70 and 72 for the forty who passed.

np.vstack means stack vertically — put the failing forty on top of the passing forty to make one table of eighty rows and two columns. np.r_ builds the answer column the same way: forty zeros, then forty ones.

So the shapes are X = (80, 2) and y = (80,), which is exactly what m = 80, n = 2 in the output means: m is how many students, n is how many scores each one has.

The two clouds deliberately overlap. A neat, perfectly separable dataset would let the weights grow forever and would hide everything this file is trying to show about λ.

output
m = 80, n = 2, positives = 40

The textbook 1/(1+np.exp(-z)) overflows for very negative z, because e^1000 does not fit in a float. The two branches here are algebraically identical and each avoids the overflow the other would hit. Libraries all do some version of this; it is worth seeing once.

def sigmoid(z):
    """1 / (1 + e^-z), written so it never overflows.

    For very negative z, e^-z is astronomically large and np.exp warns.
    The two branches are algebraically identical; each avoids the overflow
    the other would hit.
    """
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    out = np.empty_like(z)
    pos = z >= 0
    out[pos] = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z[pos]))
    ez = np.exp(z[~pos])
    out[~pos] = ez / (1.0 + ez)
    return out

print("sigmoid(-1000) =", sigmoid(-1000.0), " (no overflow warning)")
print("sigmoid([-2, 0, 2]) =", np.round(sigmoid([-2, 0, 2]), 4))
print("g(-z) == 1 - g(z):", np.allclose(sigmoid(-3.7), 1 - sigmoid(3.7)))
Line by line, in plain words

This is the one genuinely new idea in the file. The weighted sum can come out as any number at all. A probability may not — it has to sit between 0 and 1. The sigmoid is the funnel between them.

  1.0 |                        _____----------
      |                  __--
      |               _--
  0.5 |- - - - - - - -*
      |            _--
      |       __---
  0.0 |------
      +----------------------------------------
           negative        0        positive
                        z
Very negative goes to 0, very positive goes to 1, and it passes through exactly 0.5 at z = 0.
what this block actually printed
sigmoid(−2)0.1192well below the middle — probably no
sigmoid(0)0.5exactly undecided
sigmoid(2)0.8808well above — probably yes
sigmoid(−1000)0.0and no overflow warning, which is the point of the next bit

Notice it is symmetric: 0.1192 and 0.8808 add to exactly 1. That is the last line of the output checking itself — the chance of passing at z and the chance of failing at −z are the same number.

Now, why is the function written in two halves? The textbook formula is one line:

1 / (1 + exp(-z))the version in every textbook, and it breaks

Try it at z = −1000. The machine has to work out exp(1000) — a number with 435 digits. It does not fit in a float. It overflows and warns, and you get nonsense.

so the code splits in two, and each half is safe where it is used
When z is 0 or above
1 / (1 + exp(-z))
The exponent −z is negative or zero, so exp stays small and safe.
When z is below 0
exp(z) / (1 + exp(z))
Now the exponent z is the negative one, so again exp stays small and safe.
The pointThese are not two different formulas. Multiply the top and bottom of the first by exp(z) and you get the second exactly. Same maths, rearranged so that whichever side of zero you are on, the thing being exponentiated is never positive.

You will meet a second spelling of this. File 03 writes it as a single np.where. It is not a different sigmoid — the two agree to the last bit over 20,001 values from −800 to +800, and at ±10,000 too.

But it is safe for a different reason, and the difference is worth knowing. np.where does not pick a branch and skip the other: it computes both branches over the whole array, then chooses element by element. So putting the obvious two formulas inside an np.where would still overflow — the doomed half runs anyway. File 03 uses -|z| in both branches, which is never positive whichever side you are on.

same answer, two different ways of avoiding the same cliff
This page's version is safe because…
each formula only ever runs on the half of the data it suits.
File 03's version is safe because…
neither formula can overflow in the first place.

Two details. np.clip keeps the log away from 0, where it would return −inf. And the penalty is on w only — never on b, because shrinking the model's baseline towards zero buys nothing.

def compute_cost(X, y, w, b, lam=0.0):
    """Average log loss, plus the regularization term on w only (never b)."""
    f = sigmoid(X @ w + b)
    eps = 1e-12                                  # keeps log() away from 0
    f = np.clip(f, eps, 1 - eps)
    loss = -(y * np.log(f) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - f))
    return float(loss.mean() + (lam / (2 * len(y))) * np.sum(w ** 2))
Line by line, in plain words

The cost answers one question: how bad is this set of weights? One number, so that two candidate models can be compared.

File 01 squared the miss. That will not do here. Suppose the model says “99% sure this student passed” and the student failed. The plain error is 0.99, which sounds small. It is a catastrophe, and the cost has to say so.

the log lossloss = -( y * log(f) + (1 - y) * log(1 - f) )“minus, y times log f, plus one minus y times log one minus f”

It looks forbidding and it is really two cases wearing one coat. Because y is always 0 or 1, one of the two halves is always multiplied by zero and disappears.

one of these two is always zero
If the student PASSED  (y = 1)
1 - y is 0, so the right half vanishes.
Only -log(f) is left.
If the student FAILED  (y = 0)
y is 0, so the left half vanishes.
Only -log(1-f) is left.
the student passed. What each guess costs
said 0.99→cost 0.01confident and right — almost free
said 0.60→cost 0.51unsure — charged a little
said 0.01→cost 4.61confident and wrong — 460× more
The pointRight and confident is nearly free. Unsure costs a little. Wrong and confident costs enormously — and the cost runs off towards infinity as the model approaches total certainty about something false. That asymmetry is not a side effect. It is the entire reason this cost exists instead of the squared error.

Which is also why the next two lines are there:

eps = 1e-12 f = np.clip(f, eps, 1 - eps)keep f away from the cliff edges

log(0) is undefined — it heads for minus infinity — so a probability that rounds all the way to 0 or 1 would poison the whole sum. np.clip nudges them to 0.000000000001 and 0.999999999999: far enough from the edge to be safe, close enough to change no answer you care about.

The last term is the fine for large weights:

(lam / (2 * len(y))) * np.sum(w ** 2)λ times how big the weights have grown
The pointNotice what is not in that term: b. The bias is never penalised. Shrinking w flattens the model’s confidence, which is the point; shrinking b would only drag the boundary towards the origin, for no reason at all.

Compare this line with the linear-regression version: (X.T @ err) / m. Character for character the same. Only the definition of err changed, because a sigmoid's derivative and a log's derivative cancel exactly. That cancellation is the real reason these two are always paired.

def compute_gradient(X, y, w, b, lam=0.0):
    """Character for character the same as linear regression, except f."""
    m = len(y)
    err = sigmoid(X @ w + b) - y
    dj_dw = (X.T @ err) / m + (lam / m) * w      # penalty derivative is (lam/m)w
    dj_db = float(err.sum() / m)                 # b is NOT regularized
    return dj_dw, dj_db
Line by line, in plain words

Here is the payoff for all of file 01. Read these two lines next to the linear regression ones and they are character for character the same:

err = sigmoid(X @ w + b) - y — the only difference in the entire gradient is that sigmoid(...) sits where the bare line used to be. That is not a coincidence or a convenience; it falls out of the algebra, and it is why the log loss is the “right” cost for a sigmoid rather than an arbitrary one.

X.T @ err is the same weighted sum you met in file 01: each student's miss multiplied by that student's scores, added up. .T is the transpose — it turns the table on its side so the shapes line up: (2, 80) @ (80,) → (2,), one slope per weight.

+ (lam / m) * w is the penalty's own slope. A large weight gets a large push back towards zero; a weight already near zero is barely touched.

And dj_db has no lam term at all, matching the cost: b is never regularized.

Same checker as file 01, now with λ switched on, so the penalty's derivative (λ/m)·w is verified too.

def numeric_gradient(f, theta, eps=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros_like(theta, dtype=float)
    for i in range(theta.size):
        up, dn = theta.astype(float).copy(), theta.astype(float).copy()
        up[i] += eps; dn[i] -= eps
        g[i] = (f(up) - f(dn)) / (2 * eps)
    return g

Xs = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)                  # scale, as always
w0, b0, lam = np.array([0.3, -0.2]), 0.1, 1.5
ana, _ = compute_gradient(Xs, y, w0, b0, lam)
num = numeric_gradient(lambda w: compute_cost(Xs, y, w, b0, lam), w0)
print("\nanalytic dj_dw:", np.round(ana, 8))
print("numeric  dj_dw:", np.round(num, 8))
print("max difference:", f"{np.max(np.abs(ana - num)):.3e}")
Line by line, in plain words

This block is a test, and it is the reason to trust everything after it.

There are two ways to find a slope. You can do the calculus — that is compute_gradient. Or you can measure it: nudge one weight up by a hair, nudge it down by a hair, see how much the cost moved, and divide. That is numeric_gradient, and eps = 1e-6 is the size of the hair.

The measured version is far too slow to train with — it re-runs the whole cost twice for every single weight — but it needs no calculus, so it cannot repeat a calculus mistake. If the two agree, the derivative was differentiated correctly.

Look at the output. Both come out as [-0.33510702, -0.36844957] and the largest disagreement is 6.785e-11 — a decimal point followed by ten zeros. That is the noise floor of floating-point arithmetic, not an error.

This is a real professional habit, not a teaching exercise. A wrong gradient does not crash. It trains happily and converges to the wrong answer, and this ten-line check is how you find out.

output
analytic dj_dw: [-0.33510702 -0.36844957]
numeric  dj_dw: [-0.33510702 -0.36844957]
max difference: 6.785e-11

Nothing new — the loop is identical to linear regression.

def gradient_descent(X, y, alpha, iters, lam=0.0):
    w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0
    for i in range(iters):
        dw, db = compute_gradient(X, y, w, b, lam)
        w, b = w - alpha * dw, b - alpha * db
        if i % (iters // 5) == 0:
            print(f"  iter {i:5d}  cost {compute_cost(X, y, w, b, lam):.5f}")
    return w, b

print("\ntraining (lambda = 0):")
w, b = gradient_descent(Xs, y, alpha=0.5, iters=5000)
print(f"learned w = {np.round(w, 4)}  b = {b:.4f}")
Line by line, in plain words

w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0 starts every weight at zero. Follow what that means on the first iteration: z is 0 for every student, so sigmoid(0) is 0.5, so the model's opening position is “every student has a 50-50 chance”. It knows nothing, and it says so.

Then the loop, three lines, repeated 5,000 times: work out which way is downhill, step that way, repeat.

Xs = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0), back in the check block, is why it works at all. Raw exam scores run 20–100; after scaling they run about −2 to +2. Without that, one weight needs a big step and the other a small one, and a single alpha cannot suit both.

The printed cost tells the story: 0.568 at the start, 0.121 by iteration 1,000, and then 0.12139 forever. It has stopped improving by a fifth of the way in — the remaining 4,000 iterations change nothing. The final weights are w = [4.72, 2.85] and b = −0.095, meaning the first exam matters roughly 1.7 times as much as the second.

  iter  3000  cost 0.12139

The threshold at 0.5 is a separate decision made after training. The model outputs a probability; turning it into a label is your choice, and moving it trades precision against recall.

prob = sigmoid(Xs @ w + b)
pred = (prob >= 0.5).astype(int)                 # the threshold is a separate choice
acc = (pred == y).mean()
tp = int(((pred == 1) & (y == 1)).sum()); fp = int(((pred == 1) & (y == 0)).sum())
fn = int(((pred == 0) & (y == 1)).sum()); tn = int(((pred == 0) & (y == 0)).sum())
prec = tp / (tp + fp); rec = tp / (tp + fn)
print(f"\naccuracy {acc:.3f}   TP {tp}  FP {fp}  FN {fn}  TN {tn}")
print(f"precision {prec:.3f}   recall {rec:.3f}   F1 {2*prec*rec/(prec+rec):.3f}")
Line by line, in plain words

The model outputs probabilities. A decision needs a yes or a no, so (prob >= 0.5) draws the line. The comment in the file — “the threshold is a separate choice” — is the important part: 0.5 is not something the model learned. You chose it, and you may choose differently.

.astype(int) just turns True/False into 1/0 so it can be compared with y.

The four counts are the four things that can happen, and they are worth saying slowly. Treating “passed” as the positive case:

  • TP = 38 — said pass, did pass. Correct.
  • TN = 38 — said fail, did fail. Correct.
  • FP = 2 — said pass, actually failed. A false alarm.
  • FN = 2 — said fail, actually passed. A miss.

Precision = 38/(38+2) = 0.95: when it says pass, how often is it right? Recall = 38/(38+2) = 0.95: of everyone who really passed, how many did it find? They are equal here only because FP and FN happen to both be 2. F1 combines them into one number, and it is 0.95 too.

Accuracy is 0.95 as well — 76 right out of 80. It agrees with the others here because the classes are balanced, forty and forty. On a lopsided problem it stops agreeing, and that is precisely when precision and recall earn their keep.

output
accuracy 0.950   TP 38  FP 2  FN 2  TN 38
precision 0.950   recall 0.950   F1 0.950

The boundary is wherever z = 0, because g(0) = 0.5. You never compute a sigmoid to find it — solve the straight line instead.

# The boundary is where z = 0, i.e. w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b = 0.
# Solve for x2:  x2 = -(w1*x1 + b) / w2
print("\ndecision boundary in scaled space:")
for x1 in [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]:
    print(f"  x1 = {x1:+.1f}  ->  x2 = {-(w[0]*x1 + b)/w[1]:+.3f}")
Line by line, in plain words

Where exactly does the model change its mind? At the probability 0.5. And sigmoid gives 0.5 at exactly one input: z = 0.

So the dividing line is wherever w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = 0. Rearranging for x₂ gives the line the code prints: x₂ = -(w₁x₁ + b) / w₂.

Three points off that line appear in the output: at x₁ = −1 the boundary is at x₂ = +1.690; at x₁ = 0 it is at +0.033; at x₁ = +1 it is at −1.623. Three points, dropping steadily — it is a straight line, sloping down.

Which is the honest limit of this model. Everything on one side is called a pass, everything on the other a fail, and the frontier between them is straight. It cannot curve around an island of failing students sitting in the middle of the passing ones.

These numbers are in scaled space, because the model was trained on scaled data. To draw the line on a chart of real exam marks you would have to undo the scaling first.

Watch ‖w‖ shrink as λ grows while accuracy holds or improves. That is regularization doing its job: the same decisions, made with less confidence, which generalises better.

print("\nwhat lambda does to the weights:")
print(f"{'lambda':>8}  {'|w|':>8}  {'train acc':>9}")
for lam in [0.0, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]:
    wl, bl = np.zeros(n), 0.0
    for _ in range(3000):
        dw, db = compute_gradient(Xs, y, wl, bl, lam)
        wl, bl = wl - 0.5 * dw, bl - 0.5 * db
    a = ((sigmoid(Xs @ wl + bl) >= 0.5).astype(int) == y).mean()
    print(f"{lam:8.0f}  {np.linalg.norm(wl):8.4f}  {a:9.3f}")
print("\nbigger lambda -> smaller weights -> a flatter, more cautious model.")
Line by line, in plain words

This block runs the whole training four times with a bigger λ each time, and prints two things: how big the weights got, and how accurate it was.

np.linalg.norm(wl) is the length of the weight vector — roughly “how big are all the weights together”. Read the column down:

  • λ = 0 → |w| = 5.52, accuracy 0.950
  • λ = 1 → |w| = 2.93, accuracy 0.963
  • λ = 10 → |w| = 1.28, accuracy 0.963
  • λ = 100 → |w| = 0.32, accuracy 0.963

The weights shrink by a factor of seventeen and the accuracy goes up and stays up. That is the argument for regularization in four lines: the same decisions, made with less confidence, and the confidence was never earned in the first place.

What is actually happening: with λ = 0 nothing stops the weights growing, so the model pushes every probability towards 0.000 or 1.000 — it becomes certain. λ charges a fee for that certainty. The boundary stays in nearly the same place; the model just stops shouting about it.

Now the trap. The regularized update is w := w(1 − αλ/m) − α·gradient, so it shrinks w by a factor before every step. If αλ/m > 2 that factor goes past −1 and the weights flip sign and grow every iteration. A λ that is perfectly safe at one α diverges at another — and this is not in any lecture.

# Regularized descent shrinks w by (1 - alpha*lam/m) before every gradient step.
# If that factor goes negative, w flips sign and grows every iteration. This is
# a real trap: a lambda that is fine at one alpha diverges at another.
print("\nthe hidden constraint between alpha and lambda:")
print(f"{'alpha':>7} {'lambda':>7} {'1-a*l/m':>9}   outcome")
for alpha, lam in [(0.5, 100.0), (0.5, 320.0), (0.5, 1000.0), (0.05, 1000.0)]:
    factor = 1 - alpha * lam / m
    wl, bl = np.zeros(n), 0.0
    with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):   # divergence is the point here
        for _ in range(2000):
            dw, db = compute_gradient(Xs, y, wl, bl, lam)
            wl, bl = wl - alpha * dw, bl - alpha * db
        norm = np.linalg.norm(wl)
    state = "diverged" if not np.isfinite(norm) else f"|w| = {norm:.4f}"
    print(f"{alpha:7.2f} {lam:7.0f} {factor:9.3f}   {state}")
print("\nStable only while alpha*lambda/m < 2, i.e. alpha < 2m/lambda.")
print(f"With m = {m} and lambda = 1000 that means alpha < {2*m/1000:.3f}.")
Line by line, in plain words

The last block is the trap, and it is not in any lecture.

Look at what the regularized update does to w before the gradient is even applied. Combining the two terms gives w := w(1 − αλ/m) − α × gradient. So every step multiplies the weights by 1 − αλ/m. Call that the shrink factor.

  • factor 0.9 → the weight gently shrinks: 10 → 9 → 8.1. Fine.
  • factor −0.5 → the weight flips sign every step: 10 → −5 → 2.5. Ugly, but still shrinking.
  • factor −5.25 → it flips and grows every step. Gone.

The output walks straight through those cases. α = 0.5 with λ = 100 gives a factor of 0.375 and settles at |w| = 0.32. Push λ to 320 and the factor hits exactly −1.000, which is the knife edge: it does not blow up but it does not settle either, ending at |w| = 538. At λ = 1000 the factor is −5.25 and it diverges.

Then the last line of the block fixes it without touching λ at all: keep λ = 1000 and drop α to 0.05, and the factor is back to 0.375 and the weights land at 0.041.

So the rule: you are safe while αλ/m < 2, that is α < 2m/λ. With m = 80 and λ = 1000 that means α must be below 0.160.

The lesson to carry: α and λ are not independent knobs. A λ that is perfectly safe at one learning rate destroys the model at another, and the failure looks like “training diverged”, which sends most people hunting for a bug in the gradient.

Forward propagation

From one neuron to a whole network. The loop version and the matrix version, side by side, producing identical numbers — and a proof that without activations, depth buys nothing.

Run it yourself
cd study/scratch/code
python3 03_neural_net_forward.py

Pure NumPy — no scikit-learn, no TensorFlow. Every code block below is read straight out of that file, and the output under it is what that exact block printed when this page was built. They cannot drift apart.

By the end you will have built a general forward pass for any depth, and a network you construct by hand whose behaviour you can predict exactly.

🖼️The whole program in one picture

No training in this file — only the forward pass, so nothing is hidden behind an optimiser.

"""A neural network's forward pass from scratch — C2 W1 in NumPy.

Run me:  python3 03_neural_net_forward.py

Builds up from one neuron to a whole network, then shows the loop version and
the matrix version giving identical numbers.
"""
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(z):
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    return np.where(z >= 0, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.abs(z))),
                    np.exp(-np.abs(z)) / (1 + np.exp(-np.abs(z))))
Line by line, in plain words

One import and one function. The sigmoid here is written to be overflow-proof — see file 02's sigmoid section for why, and for why this file spells it differently.

The pointNothing in this file learns. Every weight is either written down by hand or chosen to make a point. This is forward propagation alone: given the weights, what does the network compute? File 04 answers the other half.

A neuron is a dot product wearing a squash function. Once that sentence is genuinely obvious, the rest of neural networks is bookkeeping about shapes.

def neuron(x, w, b, g=sigmoid):
    """A neuron is a dot product wearing a squash function. That is all."""
    z = np.dot(w, x) + b
    return g(z)

x = np.array([1.0, 3.0])
print("one neuron, w=[2,-1], b=0.5, x=[1,3]")
print("  z =", np.dot([2.0, -1.0], x) + 0.5)
print("  a =", round(float(neuron(x, np.array([2.0, -1.0]), 0.5)), 6))
Line by line, in plain words

A neuron, in one line of code and three of arithmetic.

z = np.dot(w, x) + b return g(z)dot, add the bias, squash

With w = [2, −1], b = 0.5, x = [1, 3]:

  1. 12 × 1 = 2
  2. 2−1 × 3 = −3
  3. 32 + (−3) = −1
  4. 4−1 + 0.5 = −0.5. That is z.
  5. 5g(−0.5) = 0.377541. That is a.
The pointThe docstring puts it best: a neuron is a dot product wearing a squash function. That is the whole of it. A network with a billion parameters is doing exactly this, a billion times.

0.377 is below 0.5, so this neuron is leaning “no”. The negative weight on the second input is what did it: a large x₂ actively pushes this neuron down.

output
one neuron, w=[2,-1], b=0.5, x=[1,3]
  z = -0.5

The obvious version: walk the units one at a time. Note that W holds each unit's weights as a column. That convention is what makes the next version work.

def dense_loop(a_in, W, b, g=sigmoid):
    """One layer, written the obvious way: one unit at a time.

    W is (n_in, n_out) — column j holds unit j's weights.
    """
    units = W.shape[1]
    a_out = np.zeros(units)
    for j in range(units):
        w = W[:, j]                       # this unit's weight vector
        a_out[j] = g(np.dot(w, a_in) + b[j])
    return a_out
Line by line, in plain words

A whole layer, written the obvious way — one neuron at a time.

for j in range(units): w = W[:, j] a_out[j] = g(np.dot(w, a_in) + b[j])
The pointW[:, j] means all rows, column j. So columns are neurons — column j holds neuron j's personal weight vector.

W.shape[1] is the number of columns, which is the number of neurons. Using [0] instead gives the number of inputs, and if the two happen to be equal — a square W — the loop runs and silently does the wrong thing.

The pointThis version is correct and it will never run on a GPU. The next section fixes that without changing a single number.

The same layer as one matrix multiply. A_in @ W is (m, n_in) @ (n_in, n_out) → (m, n_out): every example against every unit, in one operation. The next block proves the two agree.

def dense(A_in, W, b, g=sigmoid):
    """The same layer for a whole batch at once.

    A_in is (m, n_in). A_in @ W is (m, n_out): every example against every
    unit, in one operation. b is (n_out,) and broadcasts down the rows.
    """
    return g(A_in @ W + b)

W1 = np.array([[1.0, -1.0, 0.5],
               [1.0,  2.0, -1.5]])       # 2 inputs -> 3 units
b1 = np.array([-1.0, 0.0, 0.25])
loop_out = dense_loop(x, W1, b1)
mat_out = dense(x.reshape(1, -1), W1, b1)[0]
print("\nloop version  :", np.round(loop_out, 6))
print("matmul version:", np.round(mat_out, 6))
print("identical:", np.allclose(loop_out, mat_out))
Line by line, in plain words

The same layer, for a whole batch, with no loop at all.

return g(A_in @ W + b)every example against every neuron, in one operation
the check this block prints
loop version[0.952574, 0.993307, 0.022977]
matmul version[0.952574, 0.993307, 0.022977]
identicalTruenot approximately — the same numbers
The pointA_in @ W is (m, n_in) @ (n_in, n_out). The inner dimension — the input size — is summed away, which is precisely the dot product each neuron needed. The loop was never doing anything the matrix multiply cannot.

b is (n_out,) and broadcasts down the rows: one bias per neuron, applied to every example, without writing that loop either.

The pointThis is the version that runs on a GPU, and it is the entire reason the 2010s happened. Same maths, same answer, a hundred times the throughput.
output
loop version  : [0.952574 0.993307 0.022977]
matmul version: [0.952574 0.993307 0.022977]
identical: True

A network is layers feeding layers, so the whole forward pass is a for loop over pairs of parameters. Four lines, any depth.

def forward(X, params, activations):
    """Run a whole network. params is [(W1,b1), (W2,b2), ...]."""
    A = X
    for (W, b), g in zip(params, activations):
        A = dense(A, W, b, g)
    return A

relu = lambda z: np.maximum(0.0, z)
W2 = np.array([[1.5], [-2.0], [1.0]])     # 3 units -> 1 output
b2 = np.array([0.5])
net = [(W1, b1), (W2, b2)]
acts = [relu, sigmoid]

batch = np.array([[1.0, 3.0], [0.0, 0.0], [-2.0, 1.0], [4.0, -1.0]])
out = forward(batch, net, acts)
print("\nbatch of 4 through a 2-3-1 network:")
for xi, oi in zip(batch, out.ravel()):
    print(f"  x = {xi}  ->  {oi:.6f}")
Line by line, in plain words

Two layers, stacked, and a batch of four examples pushed through.

for (W, b), g in zip(params, activations): A = dense(A, W, b, g)the output of one layer becomes the input of the next
The pointThat loop is forward propagation. Three lines. Everything else in this file is either building the pieces it calls or examining what came out.

[0, 0]0.679179leaning yes
[−2, 1]0.000553very confidently no
[4, −1]0.999290very confidently yes

The network uses ReLU in the hidden layer and sigmoid at the output. That is the standard arrangement: ReLU everywhere inside, and the output activation chosen by what the task needs — here, a probability.

Line by line, in plain words

Shape bookkeeping. This section exists because shape errors are the thing that actually breaks, far more often than the maths.

  input          (4, 2)
                    |
  layer 1:  (4,2) @ (2,3) + (3,)  ->  (4, 3)
                    |
  layer 2:  (4,3) @ (3,1) + (1,)  ->  (4, 1)
                    |
  output         (4, 1)
The pointRead the middle numbers: 2 meets 2, then 3 meets 3. Those are the pairs that must match. The outer numbers — 4 and 3, then 4 and 1 — are the answer.

And read the whole journey as a sentence: 4 examples with 2 features become 4 examples with 3 hidden values, and then 4 examples with 1 answer. The 4 never changes, because you always have four examples.

Here is why activations exist, demonstrated rather than asserted. Run the same network with the identity as its activation and it produces exactly the same numbers as a single layer with W1 @ W2. Depth without non-linearity is an elaborate way of writing one matrix.

# Why activations exist: without them, depth buys nothing.
identity = lambda z: z
lin = forward(batch, net, [identity, identity])
W_eq = W1 @ W2                      # one matrix does the whole network
b_eq = b1 @ W2 + b2
collapsed = batch @ W_eq + b_eq
print("\ntwo linear layers   :", np.round(lin.ravel(), 6))
print("one equivalent layer:", np.round(collapsed.ravel(), 6))
print("identical:", np.allclose(lin, collapsed))
print("-> stacking linear layers is pointless; the non-linearity is the point.")
Line by line, in plain words

The most important experiment in the file: what happens if you remove the activations?

identity = lambda z: zan activation that does nothing at all
the network, against a SINGLE matrix computed from its weights
two linear layers[−8.75, −0.75, −12.75, 19.25]
one equivalent layer[−8.75, −0.75, −12.75, 19.25]
identicalTrue
The pointTwo linear layers are exactly one linear layer. Not similar — identical, to the last decimal, and the code proves it by building the equivalent single matrix with W1 @ W2.

So a 100-layer linear network has exactly the same expressive power as a 1-layer one, and costs a hundred times as much to run. Depth without non-linearity buys nothing whatsoever.

The pointThis is why activation functions exist. Not to squash, not to normalise — to stop the layers from collapsing into each other. Each ReLU adds a kink, and no amount of matrix multiplication can flatten a kink out.
output
two linear layers   : [ -8.75  -0.75 -12.75  19.25]
one equivalent layer: [ -8.75  -0.75 -12.75  19.25]
identical: True
-> stacking linear layers is pointless; the non-linearity is the point.

“Hidden units are feature detectors” is usually said and rarely shown. Here four units are built by hand — too cool, too hot, too short, too long — and the output unit is an AND gate with a large negative weight on each, so any detector firing vetoes the roast.

# What "hidden units are feature detectors" means, made concrete.
# Good roast = temperature in [180, 260] AND duration in [12, 15].
# Build four detectors by hand, then AND them in the output unit.
K = 60.0                      # how sharp each detector's step is
Wd = np.array([
    #  too cool   too hot   too short   too long
    [   -1.0,       1.0,      0.0,        0.0   ],   # temperature feeds units 1-2
    [    0.0,       0.0,     -4.0,        4.0   ],   # duration feeds units 3-4
])
bd = np.array([ 180.0,    -260.0,      48.0,      -60.0 ])
# unit 1 fires when -T + 180 > 0, i.e. T < 180.  unit 2 when T > 260.
# unit 3 when -4D + 48 > 0, i.e. D < 12.          unit 4 when D > 15.
Wout = np.array([[-K], [-K], [-K], [-K]])   # any detector firing vetoes the roast
bout = np.array([K / 2])                    # nothing firing -> sigmoid(K/2) = 1

coffee = [(Wd, bd), (Wout, bout)]
tests = np.array([[200., 13.9], [200., 17.0], [285., 12.5],
                  [175., 13.0], [220., 12.5], [259.9, 14.9]])
probs = forward(tests, coffee, [sigmoid, sigmoid]).ravel()
print("\nhand-built roast checker  (temp C, minutes) -> P(good)")
for (t, d), pr in zip(tests, probs):
    want = "good" if (180 <= t <= 260 and 12 <= d <= 15) else "bad"
    got = "good" if pr >= 0.5 else "bad"
    print(f"  {t:5.0f} C for {d:4.1f} min  ->  {pr:.4f}  {got:4s} (want {want}) "
          f"{'OK' if got == want else 'WRONG'}")
Line by line, in plain words

What does “hidden units are feature detectors” actually mean? This section makes it concrete by building four detectors by hand.

The rule to reproduce: a roast is good if the temperature is between 180 and 260 AND the duration is between 12 and 15 minutes.

four hand-built detectors in the hidden layer
Unit 1 — too cool?
fires when T < 180
Unit 2 — too hot?
fires when T > 260
Unit 3 — too short?
fires when D < 12
Unit 4 — too long?
fires when D > 15

The output unit gives each detector a weight of −60 and itself a bias of +30. So with nothing firing it outputs sigmoid(30) ≈ 1, and any single detector firing drags it to sigmoid(−30) ≈ 0.

The pointThat is an AND gate, built out of neurons: good roast = NOT too cool AND NOT too hot AND NOT too short AND NOT too long. Any one veto is enough.
the hand-built network against six test roasts
200 C, 13.9 min1.0000good — correct
200 C, 17.0 min0.0000too long — correct
285 C, 12.5 min0.0000too hot — correct
175 C, 13.0 min0.0000too cool — correct
220 C, 12.5 min1.0000good — correct
259.9 C, 14.9 min0.0000WRONG — it wanted good
The pointThe last row is the interesting one and it is not a bug. That roast sits 0.1° from one boundary and 0.1 min from another. A sigmoid boundary is soft: near the edge a detector outputs something between 0 and 1, so the AND gate is genuinely undecided. The next section shows this happening.

Print the hidden layer and read it directly: every row of zeros is a good roast. A trained network's hidden layer holds exactly this kind of thing, except nobody chose what the detectors would detect.

# Look at what the hidden layer actually outputs — these are the detectors.
h = dense(tests, Wd, bd, sigmoid)
print("\ninside the hidden layer  [too cool, too hot, too short, too long]")
for (t, d), row in zip(tests, h):
    print(f"  {t:5.0f} C, {d:4.1f} min -> {np.round(row, 3)}")
print("\nEvery row of zeros is a good roast. The output unit is just an AND gate:")
print("it adds -60 for every detector that fires, so one firing is enough to veto.")

# Sweep a grid and see how faithfully the network reproduces the rule.
# The grid is deliberately offset so no point lands exactly on a boundary,
# where a sigmoid is genuinely 0.5 and the answer is a coin flip.
T, D = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(150.7, 300.7, 61), np.linspace(10.13, 18.13, 41))
grid = np.c_[T.ravel(), D.ravel()]
want = ((grid[:, 0] >= 180) & (grid[:, 0] <= 260) &
        (grid[:, 1] >= 12) & (grid[:, 1] <= 15))
# distance to the nearest boundary, in the units each detector actually sees
edge = np.minimum(np.minimum(np.abs(grid[:, 0] - 180), np.abs(grid[:, 0] - 260)),
                  4.0 * np.minimum(np.abs(grid[:, 1] - 12), np.abs(grid[:, 1] - 15)))

print(f"\nswept {len(grid)} grid points. Sharpening the DETECTORS (not the output):")
print(f"{'sharpness':>10} {'match':>8}   widest disagreement from the boundary")
for sharp in [1.0, 3.0, 10.0]:
    c2 = [(Wd * sharp, bd * sharp), (Wout, bout)]
    got = forward(grid, c2, [sigmoid, sigmoid]).ravel() >= 0.5
    agree = got == want
    band = edge[~agree].max() if (~agree).any() else 0.0
    print(f"{sharp:10.0f} {100 * agree.mean():7.2f}%   {band:.3f}")
print("\nA sigmoid boundary is SOFT: near the edge the unit outputs something")
print("between 0 and 1, so the AND gate is undecided. Steeper weights shrink")
print("that band but never remove it — which is exactly why the network can")
print("express 'probably good' instead of only 'good' or 'bad'.")

The pointEvery row of zeros is a good roast. The raw input was [temperature, duration]; the hidden layer has transformed it into [too cool?, too hot?, too short?, too long?] — which is a far more useful description of the same coffee.

That transformation is what learned features means. Here they were built by hand so you can see them; in a trained network the same kind of thing emerges from gradient descent, without anyone naming it.

The pointAnd the last row explains the WRONG answer above: 0.475 and 0.401 — two detectors each about half-firing. Together they add up to enough veto to tip the output past 0.5, even though neither alone would have. The grid sweep that follows shows that sharpening the weights shrinks this uncertain band but can never remove it — which is exactly what lets a network say “probably good” instead of only “good” or “bad”.

Backpropagation

Every gradient derived by hand and checked numerically, then used to train a network on XOR — the smallest problem a linear model cannot solve. No autodiff anywhere.

Run it yourself
cd study/scratch/code
python3 04_backprop.py

Pure NumPy — no scikit-learn, no TensorFlow. Every code block below is read straight out of that file, and the output under it is what that exact block printed when this page was built. They cannot drift apart.

By the end you will have built a complete two-layer network with hand-derived gradients, a gradient checker that passes, and a demonstration of why it fails on a ReLU kink.

🖼️The whole program in one picture

This is the file that turns backprop from a word into arithmetic. Nothing here calls a library that computes a derivative for you.

"""Backpropagation from scratch — C2 W2, with no autodiff anywhere.

Run me:  python3 04_backprop.py

Every gradient here is derived by hand and then checked numerically. The
network learns XOR, which is the smallest problem a linear model cannot solve.
"""
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def sigmoid(z):
    return np.where(z >= 0, 1 / (1 + np.exp(-np.abs(z))),
                    np.exp(-np.abs(z)) / (1 + np.exp(-np.abs(z))))
Line by line, in plain words

Forward propagation asks: what did the network predict? Backpropagation asks the other question: which weight caused the mistake, and by how much?

The pointThis file derives every gradient by hand, checks each one numerically, and then uses them to train a network on XOR — the smallest problem a straight line cannot solve.

Start with the smallest graph that has anything to say. Forward: compute a, then J. Backward: work out how much J changes per unit of a, then multiply by how much a changes per unit of w. That multiplication is the chain rule, and it is all backprop ever does.

# Start with the smallest possible graph:  a = wx + b,  J = (a - y)^2
w, b, x, y = 3.0, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0
a = w * x + b
J = (a - y) ** 2
dJ_da = 2 * (a - y)          # derivative of the square
dJ_dw = dJ_da * x            # chain rule: da/dw = x
dJ_db = dJ_da * 1            # da/db = 1
print("forward :  a =", a, " J =", J)
print("backward:  dJ/da =", dJ_da, " dJ/dw =", dJ_dw, " dJ/db =", dJ_db)
eps = 1e-6
num = (((w + eps) * x + b - y) ** 2 - ((w - eps) * x + b - y) ** 2) / (2 * eps)
print("numeric dJ/dw =", round(num, 6), " -> matches:", abs(num - dJ_dw) < 1e-5)
Line by line, in plain words

Before touching a network, do the whole thing on one node, where you can follow every number.

  1. 1Forward: with the given w, b and x, the node outputs a = 7.0, and the cost comes out J = 4.0.
  2. 2Backward: ∂J/∂a = 4.0 — how much J moves if a moves.
  3. 3Then ∂J/∂w = 8.0 and ∂J/∂b = 4.0, by multiplying along the path.
  4. 4Check it numerically: nudge w, measure. 8.0. Matches.
The pointNotice the direction. The forward pass went left to right and produced one number. The backward pass starts at that number and goes right to left, and each step is just a multiplication by a local slope.

Everything after this is the same four steps with more nodes. Nothing new is introduced — only more of it.

output
forward :  a = 7.0  J = 4.0
backward:  dJ/da = 4.0  dJ/dw = 8.0  dJ/db = 4.0
numeric dJ/dw = 8.0  -> matches: True

A sigmoid's derivative written in terms of its own output, a(1−a), is why the forward pass caches activations: the backward pass reuses them rather than recomputing. Note the slope collapses at both ends — that is saturation, and it is what ReLU was introduced to avoid.

# The three derivatives every backward pass in this course is built from.
def d_sigmoid(a):
    """Given the OUTPUT a of a sigmoid, its derivative is a(1-a).

    Expressing it in terms of a rather than z is why the forward pass caches
    its activations: the backward pass reuses them instead of recomputing.
    """
    return a * (1 - a)

def d_relu(z):
    return (z > 0).astype(float)

for a in [0.1, 0.5, 0.9]:
    print(f"  sigmoid output {a}  ->  slope {d_sigmoid(a):.4f}")
print("  slope is largest at 0.5 and vanishes at both ends — that is the")
print("  saturation problem ReLU was introduced to avoid.")
Line by line, in plain words

Backprop needs the slope of every activation function. The sigmoid's has a famously tidy form — and a famous problem.

g'(z) = g(z) · (1 - g(z))the slope, computed from the OUTPUT you already have
the sigmoid's slope at three points
output 0.1slope 0.0900near the flat left end
output 0.5slope 0.2500the steepest it ever gets
output 0.9slope 0.0900near the flat right end
The pointTwo things to take from those numbers. First, you never need z — the slope is computable from the activation the forward pass already stored, which is why forward values are kept.

Second, and much more important: the slope peaks at 0.25 and vanishes at both ends. Every layer multiplies the gradient by at most 0.25. Stack ten sigmoid layers and the first one receives at most 0.2510 ≈ 0.00000095 of the signal.

The pointThat is the saturation problem, and it is exactly what ReLU was introduced to avoid: ReLU's slope on the positive side is exactly 1, so gradients pass through undiminished however deep the stack.
output
  sigmoid output 0.1  ->  slope 0.0900
  sigmoid output 0.5  ->  slope 0.2500
  sigmoid output 0.9  ->  slope 0.0900
  slope is largest at 0.5 and vanishes at both ends — that is the
  saturation problem ReLU was introduced to avoid.

Same forward pass as file 03, except it now returns a cache. Every value stored here is needed on the way back.

def forward(X, P):
    """Forward pass that CACHES everything the backward pass will need."""
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = P
    Z1 = X @ W1 + b1
    A1 = np.maximum(0.0, Z1)          # ReLU hidden layer
    Z2 = A1 @ W2 + b2
    A2 = sigmoid(Z2)                  # sigmoid output
    return A2, (X, Z1, A1, Z2, A2)

def cost(A2, y):
    eps = 1e-12
    f = np.clip(A2.ravel(), eps, 1 - eps)
    return float(-np.mean(y * np.log(f) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - f)))
Line by line, in plain words

The forward pass, written so that it returns its intermediates rather than just the answer.

The pointThat is the only difference from file 03. The backward pass needs every value the forward pass computed, so the forward pass must hand them back rather than throwing them away.

This is also why training uses far more memory than prediction. A prediction can discard each layer's output as soon as the next layer has consumed it; training cannot discard anything until the backward pass has been all the way through. When you run out of GPU memory, this is why, and halving the batch size is the first thing to try.

The whole algorithm, right to left. The one piece worth pausing on: dZ2 = (A2 − y)/m. For a sigmoid output with log loss, the sigmoid's derivative and the log's derivative cancel completely — the same cancellation you saw in logistic regression, and the reason that pairing is universal.

def backward(cache, y, P):
    """Derived by hand, right to left.

    The one piece of magic: for a sigmoid output with log loss, dJ/dZ2
    simplifies all the way down to (A2 - y)/m. The sigmoid's derivative and
    the log's derivative cancel exactly. That cancellation is why this pair
    is always used together.
    """
    X, Z1, A1, Z2, A2 = cache
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = P
    m = X.shape[0]

    dZ2 = (A2 - y.reshape(-1, 1)) / m          # (m, 1)
    dW2 = A1.T @ dZ2                           # (h, m) @ (m, 1) -> (h, 1)
    db2 = dZ2.sum(axis=0)                      # (1,)

    dA1 = dZ2 @ W2.T                           # (m, 1) @ (1, h) -> (m, h)
    dZ1 = dA1 * d_relu(Z1)                     # ReLU passes gradient only where z > 0
    dW1 = X.T @ dZ1                            # (n, m) @ (m, h) -> (n, h)
    db1 = dZ1.sum(axis=0)                      # (h,)
    return [dW1, db1, dW2, db2]
Line by line, in plain words

The backward pass. Read it as the chain rule, walked from the end.

  1. 1Start at the output with ∂J/∂J = 1.
  2. 2At each layer, multiply by that layer's local slope — how much its output moves when its input moves.
  3. 3On the way past each weight, that running product is that weight's gradient.
  4. 4Pass what is left to the layer before, and repeat.
The pointThe key insight: each node only needs to know its own little multiplier. No node knows anything about the network as a whole, and none of them needs to. The chain rule assembles the global answer out of purely local facts.

And this is why it is cheap. One forward pass plus one backward pass gives you every gradient, no matter how many parameters there are. Nudging each parameter separately would cost one forward pass each — a million passes for a million parameters, instead of two.

Four gradients, four checks, all agreeing to about 1e-10. This is the test that tells you a hand-derived backward pass is right, and it is worth writing before you trust any network you built yourself.

X = np.array([[0., 0.], [0., 1.], [1., 0.], [1., 1.]])
y = np.array([0., 1., 1., 0.])                  # XOR
h = 8
def init(seed=2):
    """He initialisation: variance 2/fan_in keeps ReLU activations from dying.

    The biases are small random numbers, NOT zeros. With zero biases every
    hidden unit sees z = 0 for the input [0, 0], which is exactly the kink in
    ReLU — where the derivative does not exist and a numeric gradient check
    disagrees with the analytic one for a genuine mathematical reason.
    """
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return [r.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / 2), (2, h)), r.normal(0, 0.1, h),
            r.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / h), (h, 1)), r.normal(0, 0.1, 1)]

P = init()
A2, cache = forward(X, P)
grads = backward(cache, y, P)

def numeric_grads(P, i, eps=1e-6):
    g = np.zeros_like(P[i], dtype=float)
    flat = g.reshape(-1)
    for k in range(P[i].size):
        up = [p.copy() for p in P]; dn = [p.copy() for p in P]
        up[i].reshape(-1)[k] += eps
        dn[i].reshape(-1)[k] -= eps
        flat[k] = (cost(forward(X, up)[0], y) - cost(forward(X, dn)[0], y)) / (2 * eps)
    return g

print("\ngradient check — hand-derived vs numerical:")
for i, name in enumerate(["dW1", "db1", "dW2", "db2"]):
    n = numeric_grads(P, i)
    diff = np.max(np.abs(grads[i] - n))
    rel = diff / max(1e-12, np.max(np.abs(grads[i])) + np.max(np.abs(n)))
    print(f"  {name}: max abs diff {diff:.3e}   relative {rel:.3e}   "
          f"{'PASS' if rel < 1e-6 else 'FAIL'}")
Line by line, in plain words

Every hand-derived gradient, checked against a numerical measurement. This is the block that makes the rest trustworthy.

max absolute difference between hand-derived and numerical
dW17.6e−11PASS
db17.2e−11PASS
dW28.1e−11PASS
db23.2e−11PASS
The pointEleven decimal places. That is the noise floor of floating-point arithmetic, not agreement-by-luck. The hand-derived calculus is right.

Do this on any network you write by hand, once, before training. A wrong gradient does not crash — it trains, converges to something, and quietly gives you a worse model than you should have had. There is no other symptom.

The pointTurn it off before real training, though. The numerical version re-runs the entire cost twice per parameter, which is exactly the cost backprop exists to avoid.

Now break it deliberately. With biases at exactly zero, every hidden unit sees z = 0 for the input [0, 0] — precisely the kink where ReLU has no derivative. The analytic gradient picks the flat side; the numerical one averages across the corner. Neither is wrong, and the check fails for an honest mathematical reason. This is why the initialiser puts the biases slightly off zero.

# Now break it on purpose. Zero biases put every unit exactly on the ReLU kink
# for the input [0, 0], and the gradient check fails — correctly.
Pz = [P[0].copy(), np.zeros(h), P[2].copy(), np.zeros(1)]
_, cz = forward(X, Pz)
gz = backward(cz, y, Pz)
nz = numeric_grads(Pz, 1)
print("\nwith biases at exactly zero, db1 analytic vs numeric:")
print("  analytic:", np.round(gz[1], 6))
print("  numeric :", np.round(nz, 6))
print(f"  max diff: {np.max(np.abs(gz[1] - nz)):.3e}  <- a REAL disagreement")
print("  ReLU has no derivative at z = 0. The analytic version picks the flat")
print("  side; the numeric version averages across the kink. Neither is wrong.")
print("  This is why gradient checks on ReLU nets need biases off the kink.")
Line by line, in plain words

Now the interesting failure. This block deliberately sets the biases to exactly zero and re-runs the check.

the same check, now failing
analytic[0.117, 0, −0.002, 0, 0.145, 0.126, −0.001, −0.011]
numeric[0.086, 0.024, 0.062, −0.051, 0.091, 0.079, 0.025, −0.007]
max difference6.4e−02a REAL disagreement
The pointThis is not a bug in either version. ReLU has no derivative at exactly z = 0. It is a kink: the slope is 0 on one side and 1 on the other, and at the point itself there is no single answer.
two defensible answers to a question with no answer
The analytic version
picks the flat side — it applies the rule z > 0, so z = 0 counts as 0.
The numeric version
averages across the kink — it steps to both sides and divides, landing somewhere in between.
The pointNeither is wrong. And in practice it does not matter: hitting z exactly zero has probability zero once weights are random, and the failure here had to be engineered by setting every bias to 0 deliberately.

It is worth seeing, though, because it is the one situation where a gradient check fails on correct code — and knowing that saves you from hunting a bug that is not there.

Full training loop: forward, backward, step, repeat. The cost falls from 0.95 to about 5e-5.

print("\ntraining on XOR:")
P = init(seed=2)
alpha = 1.0
for it in range(8001):
    A2, cache = forward(X, P)
    g = backward(cache, y, P)
    for k in range(4):
        P[k] = P[k] - alpha * g[k]
    if it % 2000 == 0:
        print(f"  iter {it:5d}  cost {cost(A2, y):.6f}")

A2, _ = forward(X, P)
print("\n  input    target   predicted")
for xi, yi, pi in zip(X, y, A2.ravel()):
    print(f"  {xi}   {yi:.0f}       {pi:.4f}   {'OK' if (pi >= .5) == (yi == 1) else 'WRONG'}")

The control experiment. Train the same data with no hidden layer and it sticks at exactly 0.5 for all four inputs, forever, because XOR is not linearly separable. The hidden layer is not a performance tweak — it is the thing that makes the problem solvable at all.

# XOR is not linearly separable — prove a network with NO hidden layer fails.
print("\nsame problem with no hidden layer (plain logistic regression):")
w1, b1 = np.zeros(2), 0.0
for _ in range(20000):
    f = sigmoid(X @ w1 + b1)
    err = f - y
    w1 -= 1.0 * (X.T @ err) / len(y)
    b1 -= 1.0 * err.mean()
pred = sigmoid(X @ w1 + b1)
print("  predictions:", np.round(pred, 4), " -> all stuck near 0.5")
print(f"  accuracy {(((pred >= .5).astype(float)) == y).mean():.2f} — no better than guessing.")
print("  The hidden layer is not an optimisation. It is what makes XOR solvable.")

"""Softmax and multi-class classification from scratch — C2 W2.

Run me:  python3 05_softmax.py

Includes the numerical-stability trick that `from_logits=True` uses, shown
by breaking the naive version first.
"""
import numpy as np
Line by line, in plain words

Binary classification asks “yes or no”. Multi-class asks “which one of these?” This file builds that, and then spends most of its length on the numerical problems softmax creates — because those are what from_logits=True exists to solve.

The definition, written exactly as the formula reads. It works, right up until it does not.

def softmax_naive(z):
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

print("softmax([2, 1, 0, 3]) =", np.round(softmax_naive(np.array([2., 1., 0., 3.])), 4))
print("sums to", softmax_naive(np.array([2., 1., 0., 3.])).sum())
Line by line, in plain words

Softmax written the obvious way, straight from the formula.

e = np.exp(z) return e / e.sum()exponentiate, then normalise
[2, 1, 0, 3]→[0.237, 0.087, 0.032, 0.644]and they sum to exactly 1.0
The pointTwo moves, each with one job. exp makes everything positive — probabilities cannot be negative and raw scores routinely are. Dividing by the total makes them sum to 1.

Notice the exaggeration: a score of 3 is only 1.5× a score of 2, but its probability is 2.7× larger. Exponentiating widens every gap, which is what makes softmax decisive.

output
softmax([2, 1, 0, 3]) = [0.2369 0.0871 0.0321 0.6439]
sums to 1.0

Logits in the hundreds are entirely normal in a trained network, and e^1000 is not a number a float can hold. The naive version returns nan and your training run is over.

# Now break it. Logits of a few hundred are entirely normal in a trained network.
with np.errstate(over="ignore", invalid="ignore"):
    bad = softmax_naive(np.array([1000., 999., 998.]))
print("\nnaive softmax on [1000, 999, 998]:", bad, " <- overflowed to nan")
Line by line, in plain words

Now break it. Three scores that are perfectly ordinary as numbers.

[1000, 999, 998]→[nan, nan, nan]every answer destroyed
The pointexp(1000) is a number with 435 digits. It does not fit in a float, so it becomes inf. Then inf / inf is nan — not a number — and nan spreads through every subsequent calculation like ink.

The correct answer here is perfectly reasonable: [0.665, 0.245, 0.090]. Nothing about the maths is extreme. Only the intermediate step was.

output
naive softmax on [1000, 999, 998]: [nan nan nan]  <- overflowed to nan

The fix is one line, and it is free: softmax(z + c) = softmax(z) for any constant c, because e^c cancels top and bottom. Choose c = −max(z) and the largest exponent becomes e⁰ = 1, so nothing can overflow. The shift invariance is proved numerically two lines down.

def softmax(z, axis=-1):
    """Subtract the max first. Algebraically identical, numerically safe.

    softmax(z + c) == softmax(z) for any constant c, because e^c cancels
    from the top and the bottom. Choosing c = -max(z) makes the largest
    exponent e^0 = 1, so nothing can overflow.
    """
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    z = z - z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)

print("stable softmax on [1000, 999, 998]:", np.round(softmax(np.array([1000., 999., 998.])), 4))
print("shift invariance:  softmax([2,1,0]) ==", np.round(softmax(np.array([2., 1., 0.])), 6))
print("                   softmax([12,11,10]) ==", np.round(softmax(np.array([12., 11., 10.])), 6))
Line by line, in plain words

The fix is one subtraction, and it works because of a property worth knowing.

e = np.exp(z - np.max(z)) return e / e.sum()subtract the largest first
shift invariance, demonstrated
softmax([2, 1, 0])[0.665241, 0.244728, 0.090031]
softmax([12, 11, 10])[0.665241, 0.244728, 0.090031]identical
The pointSoftmax depends only on the DIFFERENCES between the scores. Adding a constant to every score multiplies the top and the bottom by the same factor, which cancels exactly.

So subtracting the maximum is free — it cannot change the answer. And afterwards the largest exponent is exp(0) = 1 and everything else is smaller, so overflow is impossible. Now [1000, 999, 998] returns [0.6652, 0.2447, 0.0900] correctly.

The pointEvery real softmax implementation does this. It is not an optimisation; it is the difference between working and not.
output
stable softmax on [1000, 999, 998]: [0.6652 0.2447 0.09  ]
shift invariance:  softmax([2,1,0]) == [0.665241 0.244728 0.090031]
                   softmax([12,11,10]) == [0.665241 0.244728 0.090031]

Now the other half. Computing the probability and then its log loses precision twice, and once a probability underflows to zero the log is −inf and there is no gradient. Computing z − log Σ e^z directly never forms the tiny number at all. This is exactly what from_logits=True switches on.

def log_softmax(z, axis=-1):
    """log(softmax(z)) without ever forming softmax(z).

    log(e^z_i / sum e^z_j) = z_i - log(sum e^z_j). Computing it this way never
    creates the tiny probability that log() would then have to rescue.
    """
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float)
    m = z.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    return z - m - np.log(np.exp(z - m).sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True))

# A gap of ~750 in the logits is enough: e^-750 is below the smallest float64,
# so the probability underflows to exactly 0 and log(0) is -inf.
z = np.array([400., 0., -400.])
with np.errstate(divide="ignore"):
    p_first = softmax(z)
    naive_log = np.log(p_first)
print("\nsoftmax([400, 0, -400])   :", p_first, " <- the last one underflowed to 0")
print("then log of that          :", naive_log, " <- -inf, and no gradient")
print("direct log_softmax        :", np.round(log_softmax(z), 1), " <- still usable")
print("Same maths, different order of operations, and only one of them survives.")
Line by line, in plain words

A second, subtler failure — and this one the max-subtraction does not fix.

  1. 1softmax([400, 0, -400]) gives [1.0, 1.9e−174, 0.0]. The last one underflowed to exactly zero.
  2. 2Then take the log: [0, −400, −inf].
  3. 3−inf. And a gradient of inf is no gradient at all — training is over.

The fix is to never build the probability in the first place:

same maths, different order of operations
softmax then log[0, −400, −inf]destroyed
direct log_softmax[0, −400, −800]still usable
The pointSame maths, different order of operations, and only one of them survives. If the tiny number is never formed, it can never round to zero.
The pointThis is exactly what from_logits=True does in Keras: it tells the loss to take the raw scores and apply the rearranged formula itself, rather than accepting probabilities that have already been damaged.
output
softmax([400, 0, -400])   : [1.0000000e+000 1.9151696e-174 0.0000000e+000]  <- the last one underflowed to 0
then log of that          : [   0. -400.  -inf]  <- -inf, and no gradient
direct log_softmax        : [   0. -400. -800.]  <- still usable
Same maths, different order of operations, and only one of them survives.

Only the true class's log-probability enters the loss. That is the −log(a_y) formula, written with fancy indexing instead of a loop.

def cross_entropy(logits, y):
    """Mean loss over a batch. y holds integer class indices.

    Only the true class's log-probability enters the loss — that is the
    "pick one entry" that the -log(a_y) formula describes.
    """
    ls = log_softmax(logits, axis=1)
    return float(-ls[np.arange(len(y)), y].mean())
Line by line, in plain words

Cross-entropy, and why it is simpler than it looks.

loss = -log( p[true_class] )only the true class appears
The pointThe full formula sums over all classes with a one-hot y — but y is 0 everywhere except the true class, so every other term is multiplied by zero and vanishes. What is left is one logarithm.

So the model is scored purely on how much probability it gave to the right answer. Give it 0.99 and the loss is 0.01. Give it 0.01 and the loss is 4.61. It is the same shape as the binary log loss in file 02, extended to more than two options.

softmax(z) − onehot(y), divided by m. Beautifully simple, and the same shape of answer as the sigmoid case for the same reason: the messy derivatives cancel. Verified numerically underneath.

def grad_logits(logits, y):
    """dJ/dz for softmax + cross-entropy is (softmax(z) - onehot(y)) / m.

    Exactly the same shape of answer as sigmoid + log loss. The messy
    derivatives cancel, which is the real reason these pairs go together.
    """
    m = len(y)
    P = softmax(logits, axis=1)
    P[np.arange(m), y] -= 1.0
    return P / m

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
logits = rng.normal(size=(5, 4))
yv = rng.integers(0, 4, size=5)
ana = grad_logits(logits.copy(), yv)
num = np.zeros_like(ana)
eps = 1e-6
for i in range(logits.size):
    up, dn = logits.copy(), logits.copy()
    up.reshape(-1)[i] += eps; dn.reshape(-1)[i] -= eps
    num.reshape(-1)[i] = (cross_entropy(up, yv) - cross_entropy(dn, yv)) / (2 * eps)
print(f"\ngradient check: max diff {np.max(np.abs(ana - num)):.3e}  "
      f"{'PASS' if np.max(np.abs(ana - num)) < 1e-7 else 'FAIL'}")
Line by line, in plain words

Two intimidating derivatives multiply together and almost everything cancels.

dz = p - ypredicted probabilities minus the one-hot truth
hand-derived against numerical
gradient check2.805e−10PASS
The pointThat is the entire gradient. No exponentials, no logs, no special cases. The softmax derivative carries a factor of p and the log in cross-entropy contributes 1/p; they annihilate each other exactly.

Read the signs. The true class gets a negative gradient — push its score up. Every wrong class gets a positive one — push those down. The size of each push is exactly how wrong that probability was.

The pointIt is the same cancellation as sigmoid + log loss in file 02, which is why these pairs are always used together. Pair either half with something else and you lose this.
output
gradient check: max diff 2.805e-10  PASS

Three blobs, one linear softmax layer, trained by hand to 99.4%.

# Three blobs, one linear softmax classifier, trained by hand.
means = np.array([[0., 0.], [4., 4.], [8., 0.]])
X = np.vstack([rng.normal(mu, 1.1, size=(60, 2)) for mu in means])
y = np.repeat([0, 1, 2], 60)
Xs = (X - X.mean(0)) / X.std(0)
W, b = np.zeros((2, 3)), np.zeros(3)
print("\ntraining a 3-class softmax classifier:")
for it in range(3001):
    logits = Xs @ W + b
    if it % 750 == 0:
        acc = (logits.argmax(1) == y).mean()
        print(f"  iter {it:4d}  loss {cross_entropy(logits, y):.4f}  acc {acc:.3f}")
    dZ = grad_logits(logits, y)
    W -= 0.5 * (Xs.T @ dZ)
    b -= 0.5 * dZ.sum(0)
print(f"final accuracy: {(( Xs @ W + b).argmax(1) == y).mean():.4f}")
Line by line, in plain words

Train it on three classes and watch two numbers at once.

training a 3-class classifier
iter 0loss 1.0986, acc 0.333one in three — pure guessing
iter 750loss 0.0297, acc 0.994essentially solved
iter 3000loss 0.0183, acc 0.994polishing
finalaccuracy 0.9944
The point1.0986 at iteration 0 is not an arbitrary number. It is log(3) — exactly the loss you get from assigning 1/3 to every class. A 3-class model that starts anywhere else has a bug in its initialisation.

Notice accuracy reaches 0.994 by iteration 750 and then stops, while the loss keeps falling. The model is no longer changing its answers — only becoming more confident about the ones it already has.
